title: Chapter XXXI

teacherSummary.text: At Rosings, Colonel Fitzwilliam's lively talk draws Elizabeth to the piano. Darcy stands near, and she teases him about refusing to dance at Meryton. Darcy says he lacks the talent of conversing easily with strangers; Elizabeth replies that her playing would improve with practice, as his manners might. Lady Catherine interrupts with loud opinions.

vocabulary.context: My courage always rises with every attempt to intimidate me.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “intimidate”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: One who has made considerable advances in any business, art, science, or branch of learning
vocabulary.context: If I had ever learnt, I should have been a great proficient.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “proficient”: pro- (Latin pro, "forward, for") + fic (Latin facere, "to make") + -ent (Latin -ens, "one who, doing"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Darcy, it is very ungenerous in you to mention all that you knew to my disadvantage in Hertfordshire—and, give me leave to say, very impolitic too—for it is provoking me to retaliate, and such things may come out, as will shock your relations to hear.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXXI,” how does Austen show music, wit and manners? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XXXI, how does Austen develop the idea of music, wit and manners? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXXI develops the idea of music, wit and manners. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XXXI (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of music, wit and manners. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XXXI suggests about music, wit and manners. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and irony), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XXXI to complicate the reader's understanding of music, wit and manners. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXXI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of music, wit and manners responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XXXI alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of music, wit and manners follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XXXI and its treatment of music, wit and manners. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and irony, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XXXI as evidence for a larger claim about music, wit and manners in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXXI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of music, wit and manners. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: Colonel Fitzwilliam’s manners were very much admired at the parsonage, and the ladies all felt that he must add considerably to the pleasure of their engagements at Rosings. It was some days, however, before they received any invitation thither, for while there were visitors in the house, they could not be necessary; and it was not till Easter-day, almost a week after the gentlemen’s arrival, that they were honoured by such an attention, and then they were merely asked on leaving church to come there in the evening. For the last week they had seen very little of either Lady Catherine or her daughter. Colonel Fitzwilliam had called at the parsonage more than once during the time, but Mr. Darcy they had only seen at church.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Elizabeth compares manners to piano practice. Is that a fair comparison? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are intimidate, proficient, retaliate, disadvantage, applying. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “My courage always rises with every attempt to intimidate me.”” Webster's says: To make timid or fearful. Now the word history: “intimidate”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “proficient”: pro- (Latin pro, "forward, for") + fic (Latin facere, "to make") + -ent (Latin -ens, "one who, doing"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “retaliate”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Musical performance was a social display for marriageable young women. Why does this chapter matter? Elizabeth's analogy about practice suggests manners, like skills, can be learned—an idea about self-improvement. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to music, wit and manners.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Irony, Theme.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
